questions.explanation: Unlike cross-validation, bootstrapping resamples with replacement, so the same observation can appear multiple times in a sample. It isn't used to validate models the way cross-validation is, since an observation used for training could also end up in the "test" sample, inflating performance metrics.

options.text: A resampling technique that draws random samples from a dataset with replacement, so the same observation can appear multiple times in a sample.
A resampling technique that splits data into k folds and validates on each fold without replacement.
A technique that trains multiple models in sequence, each correcting the errors of the previous one.
A technique that trains multiple models in parallel on random subsets of features and averages their predictions.

questions.explanation: Cross-validation splits the training set into training and validation sets to evaluate a model without touching the test set. The most common strategy is k-fold cross-validation, where k is the number of splits.

options.text: A technique that splits the training set into training and validation folds (e.g., k-fold) to evaluate model performance.
A technique that resamples the training set with replacement, allowing the same observation to appear multiple times.
A technique that combines predictions from multiple independently trained models to reduce variance.
A technique that reduces the number of input features by keeping only the most important ones.

questions.explanation: In supervised learning the target variable can be binary, multi-class, or numerical, and the data type of that target variable determines which type of supervised problem you're solving (classification vs. regression).

options.text: A learning approach where models are trained on labeled data, and the target's type (binary, multi-class, or numeric) determines the kind of problem.
A learning approach where models find patterns in unlabeled data, such as grouping similar observations into clusters.
A learning approach where an agent learns by receiving rewards or penalties for actions in an environment.
A learning approach that reduces the dimensionality of data while preserving as much variance as possible.

questions.explanation: Bias comes from the simplifying assumptions a model makes about the data. Linear algorithms like linear/logistic regression assume a linear relationship and carry high bias; decision trees make fewer assumptions and have less bias.

options.text: Error introduced by the simplifying assumptions a model makes about the data, causing it to underfit.
Error caused by a model's sensitivity to fluctuations in the training data, causing it to overfit.
Error caused by an imbalanced distribution of classes in the training data.
Error introduced by using too few training examples to estimate model parameters reliably.

questions.explanation: Unsupervised problems provide no labeled data, only independent variables/features, so algorithms find patterns on their own. The most common type is clustering, which groups observations by similarity.

options.text: A learning approach that works with unlabeled data, finding structure such as clusters purely from the features.
A learning approach that trains on labeled examples to predict a known target variable.
A learning approach that uses trial-and-error interaction with an environment to maximize cumulative reward.
A learning approach that trains a smaller model to imitate the outputs of a larger pretrained model.

questions.explanation: Variance is the difference in estimations a model produces on different training data. High-variance models like unpruned decision trees tend to overfit; linear/logistic regression have low variance. Pruning helps optimize high-variance models.

options.text: Error caused by a model's sensitivity to fluctuations in the training data, causing it to overfit.
Error introduced by the simplifying assumptions a model makes about the data, causing it to underfit.
Error caused by noisy or mislabeled data points in the training set.
Error caused by evaluating a model on the same data it was trained on.

A CloudFront feature that caches content at edge locations closer to users.

questions.explanation: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as the time between the last backup and a failure. E.g., a backup taken 6 hours before a failure means a 6-hour RPO.

options.text: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as the time between the last backup and a failure.
The maximum acceptable time to restore a system to full operation after a disaster.
The maximum acceptable downtime a service can experience before violating its SLA.
The frequency at which a system's health checks run to detect failures.

questions.explanation: RTO is the maximum acceptable time between a disaster occurring and the system being fully restored. E.g., restoring service 3 hours after a failure is a 3-hour RTO; lower RTO generally costs more (spare hardware, faster restoration process).

options.text: The maximum acceptable time between a disaster occurring and the system being fully restored.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured back from the moment of failure.
The scheduled interval at which backups are taken, regardless of when a failure occurs.
The percentage of time a system is guaranteed to be available over a billing period.

questions.explanation: With SSE-C, the user supplies the encryption key on every PUT/GET. S3 performs the actual encryption/decryption but discards the key immediately after use and never stores it.

options.text: The user supplies the encryption key on each request; S3 performs the encryption/decryption but discards the key after use.
S3 generates and fully manages the encryption key end-to-end, including rotation, with no user involvement.
AWS KMS manages a customer master key, and S3 uses it to generate a data key for each object.
The client encrypts and decrypts the object locally, keeping the key entirely outside of S3.

questions.explanation: With SSE-S3, AWS handles both key management and the encryption/decryption process end to end. The user just uploads the unencrypted object; S3 creates, rotates, and manages a unique master key using AES-256.

options.text: S3 creates, rotates, and fully manages the encryption key internally using AES-256; the user just uploads the plain object.
The user supplies their own encryption key on every request, and S3 discards it right after use.
AWS KMS manages a customer master key used to generate a per-object data encryption key.
The client must encrypt the object before upload and decrypt it after download.

questions.explanation: AWS KMS manages a Customer Master Key (CMK), which is used to generate a per-object Data Encryption Key (DEK). S3 stores the encrypted DEK alongside the object. Using a customer-managed CMK adds rotation control, fine-grained permissions, and API-call logging/auditing.

options.text: AWS KMS manages a customer master key that's used to generate a per-object data encryption key, adding rotation control and auditing.
S3 generates, rotates, and manages the encryption key entirely on its own, with no KMS involvement.
The user must provide the encryption key on every PUT and GET request.
The client encrypts the object locally before uploading it to S3.
